title: Bioenergetics and Metabolism
description: ATP and free-energy coupling, glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and photosynthesis.
overview: Living cells are open systems far from equilibrium, and they stay there by continuously converting energy. Metabolism is the web of enzyme-catalyzed reactions that does this: catabolic pathways oxidize fuels (glucose, fats) and capture the free energy in ATP and reduced coenzymes, and anabolic pathways use ATP and reducing power to build molecules. The same few currencies, ATP, NADH/NADPH and FADH₂, link them all.

This chapter treats the thermodynamics of coupling, the oxidation of glucose through glycolysis, the citric acid cycle and the respiratory chain, and the reverse process, photosynthesis, which drives the electrons uphill with light. The emphasis is on the chemistry and on quantitative bookkeeping of free energy and ATP.
objectives: Use ΔG°′, concentrations and coupling to decide whether a biochemical reaction goes, and explain why ATP is the energy currency.
Calculate ΔG°′ of electron transfer from reduction potentials.
Write the stages of glycolysis with net products, the fate of pyruvate, and the regulation at phosphofructokinase.
Account for the products of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and the citric acid cycle.
Describe the electron transport chain, the proton-motive force and ATP synthase, and the ATP yield.
Outline the light reactions and the Calvin cycle, and calculate the efficiency of photosynthesis.

sections.title: Free energy, ATP and coupled reactions
body: In biochemistry the standard state is pH 7, so the standard free energy change is written ΔG°′ (with [H⁺] = 10⁻⁷ M and water at unit activity). The actual free energy depends on the cellular concentrations: ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln Q. A reaction with a positive ΔG°′ can proceed if Q is small enough, and an unfavorable reaction can be driven by **coupling** to a favorable one that shares an intermediate, because free energies add. The combined reaction is favorable if the sum of ΔG values is negative.

**Adenosine triphosphate (ATP)** carries three phosphate groups. The hydrolysis ATP + H₂O → ADP + Pᵢ has ΔG°′ = −30.5 kJ mol⁻¹. In a cell, where [ATP]/[ADP] is high (the ratio is kept at ~10 or more, far from equilibrium) and [Pᵢ] is low, the actual ΔG is −50 to −65 kJ mol⁻¹. The reasons for the large negative free energy are: relief of electrostatic repulsion between the negatively charged phosphates, better solvation of the products, resonance stabilization of the released phosphate (Pᵢ has four equivalent resonance forms), and ionization of the products at pH 7. ATP is an intermediate in the scale of phosphoryl-transfer potential: compounds higher on the scale (phosphoenolpyruvate −61.9, 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate −49.4, phosphocreatine −43.1 kJ mol⁻¹) can phosphorylate ADP, and ATP can phosphorylate those lower (glucose 6-phosphate, −13.8). ATP is kinetically stable (it does not hydrolyze spontaneously, with a barrier removed only by enzymes), so it is both a source of energy and a controllable one. Thioesters (acetyl-CoA, −31.4 kJ mol⁻¹) are another type of activated group donor.

example.title: Coupling: phosphorylation of glucose
example.problem: Glucose + Pᵢ → glucose 6-phosphate + H₂O has ΔG°′ = +13.8 kJ mol⁻¹. Show how the coupling to ATP hydrolysis (−30.5 kJ mol⁻¹) makes it work, and estimate K′eq.
example.solution: Glucose + ATP → glucose 6-phosphate + ADP: ΔG°′ = +13.8 − 30.5 = −16.7 kJ mol⁻¹. K′eq = exp(16,700/(8.314 × 298)) = exp(6.74) = 8.4 × 10². The reaction (hexokinase) is practically irreversible, whereas the uncoupled one has K′eq = exp(−5.57) = 3.8 × 10⁻³.

body: Most of the energy of food is released in oxidations, with electrons passed to **NAD⁺** (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide), which accepts a hydride ion (H⁻) at C4 of the nicotinamide ring to give **NADH**: the catabolic carrier, with E°′ = −0.320 V. **NADPH** (with an extra phosphate) has the same potential but is the reductant for anabolism (fatty acid synthesis, photosynthesis). **FAD** (flavin adenine dinucleotide) accepts two electrons and two protons to give **FADH₂** (E°′ about −0.22 V when bound to proteins), used when the oxidation is of C–C single bonds (succinate to fumarate). The free energy of electron transfer follows from the reduction potentials:

example.title: Oxidation of NADH by oxygen
example.problem: Using E°′(NAD⁺/NADH) = −0.320 V and E°′(½O₂/H₂O) = +0.816 V, calculate ΔG°′ for NADH + H⁺ + ½O₂ → NAD⁺ + H₂O. How many ATP (−30.5 kJ mol⁻¹) could this support at 100% efficiency?
example.solution: ΔE°′ = 0.816 − (−0.320) = 1.136 V; n = 2. ΔG°′ = −2 × 96.485 × 1.136 = −219 kJ mol⁻¹. At 100% efficiency 219/30.5 = 7.2 ATP; in reality about 2.5 ATP are made per NADH (≈ 35% efficiency under standard conditions, about 50–60% at cellular concentrations), the remainder is released as heat.

check.q: Why is ATP hydrolysis so exergonic?
check.a: Charge repulsion relief, resonance stabilization and solvation of the products
wrong: The P–O bond is unusually weak

check.q: A reaction has ΔG°′ = +20 kJ mol⁻¹. It can still proceed in the cell if…
check.a: It is coupled to a sufficiently exergonic reaction, or Q is kept low

sections.title: Glycolysis and fermentation
body: **Glycolysis** (Greek, “sugar splitting”) oxidizes one glucose (C₆) to two pyruvate (C₃) in the cytosol in ten steps, with no oxygen required. It has two phases.

list: **Investment phase** (steps 1–5): glucose is phosphorylated by **hexokinase** (ATP → ADP; irreversible), isomerized to fructose 6-phosphate, and phosphorylated again by **phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1)** (ATP → ADP) to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, then cleaved by aldolase into two triose phosphates (dihydroxyacetone phosphate, isomerized to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, G3P). Two ATP are spent per glucose.

**Payoff phase** (steps 6–10, twice per glucose): G3P is oxidized and phosphorylated by G3P dehydrogenase with NAD⁺ and Pᵢ, giving 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (a high-energy acyl phosphate) and NADH. Phosphoglycerate kinase transfers that phosphate to ADP (**substrate-level phosphorylation**), the intermediate is rearranged and dehydrated to **phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP)**, and **pyruvate kinase** transfers the phosphate of PEP to ADP to give pyruvate. Four ATP are produced.

body: Net reaction: glucose + 2 NAD⁺ + 2 ADP + 2 Pᵢ → 2 pyruvate + 2 NADH + 2 ATP + 2 H⁺ + 2 H₂O, with ΔG°′ ≈ −85 kJ mol⁻¹ (the sum of ≈ −146 kJ for the oxidation and +61 for the 2 ATP synthesized). Three steps (hexokinase, PFK-1, pyruvate kinase) have large negative ΔG and are irreversible in the cell; these are the control points and have to be bypassed in gluconeogenesis. The main control is at **PFK-1**: it is inhibited by ATP and citrate (high energy supply) and activated by AMP and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate, so the flux follows the energy state of the cell.

NAD⁺ is the limiting resource: the NADH produced must be reoxidized or glycolysis stops. With oxygen, the electrons are passed to the respiratory chain (and pyruvate enters the mitochondrion). Without oxygen, **fermentation** regenerates NAD⁺ by reducing pyruvate. In **lactate fermentation** (muscle under strenuous exercise, many bacteria) **lactate dehydrogenase** reduces pyruvate to lactate. In **alcoholic fermentation** (yeast), pyruvate decarboxylase (thiamine pyrophosphate) releases CO₂ to give acetaldehyde, which alcohol dehydrogenase reduces to ethanol. Fermentation extracts only 2 ATP per glucose (≈ 5% of the energy of the full oxidation). Many tumors ferment glucose even with oxygen present (the Warburg effect).

example.title: Why PFK-1 is regulated by ATP
example.problem: Explain in terms of the energetic needs why high ATP inhibits PFK-1 but high AMP activates it.
example.solution: When ATP is abundant, the cell needs no more; stopping the committed step of glycolysis saves glucose. When ATP is consumed, ADP is converted into ATP and AMP by adenylate kinase (2 ADP ⇌ ATP + AMP), and because the AMP level is small, a 10% fall of ATP gives a large relative rise of AMP, a sensitive signal that activates PFK-1 to restore ATP.

check.q: What is the net ATP yield of glycolysis per glucose (anaerobic)?
Why does fermentation convert pyruvate to lactate or ethanol?
check.a: To regenerate NAD⁺ so that glycolysis can continue

sections.title: The citric acid cycle
body: In the aerobic pathway pyruvate enters the **mitochondrion** (a double-membrane organelle whose inner membrane is folded into cristae; the enclosed space is the **mitochondrial matrix**), where the **pyruvate dehydrogenase complex** converts it to **acetyl-CoA**: pyruvate + CoA + NAD⁺ → acetyl-CoA + CO₂ + NADH. The reaction needs five cofactors (thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoamide, FAD, NAD⁺, coenzyme A) in three enzymes, and is irreversible: animals cannot convert acetyl-CoA back to glucose. Fatty acids are also degraded to acetyl-CoA, two carbons at a time, by β-oxidation, which makes fats an efficient fuel (palmitate gives 106 ATP, from 7 FADH₂, 7 NADH and 8 acetyl-CoA).

The **citric acid cycle** (Krebs cycle, TCA cycle) oxidizes the two carbons of the acetyl group completely to CO₂. It is a cycle: the four-carbon **oxaloacetate** is regenerated at the end, so the intermediates act as catalysts. The eight steps are:

head: Step
Reaction
Product
rows: Thioester hydrolysis drives it (ΔG°′ ≈ −32 kJ mol⁻¹)
table.caption: The citric acid cycle.

body: Per turn (per acetyl-CoA): 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP and 2 CO₂. The cycle makes little ATP directly; its function is to produce the reduced coenzymes that feed the respiratory chain. Regulation: pyruvate dehydrogenase, citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase are inhibited by NADH and ATP and activated by ADP and Ca²⁺, so the rate follows the demand. Intermediates are also drawn off for biosynthesis (citrate for fatty acids, α-ketoglutarate for amino acids), so the cycle is refilled by **anaplerotic reactions** (pyruvate carboxylase makes oxaloacetate).

check.q: How many NADH, FADH₂ and GTP are produced per turn of the citric acid cycle?
Which steps of the citric acid cycle release CO₂?

sections.title: Oxidative phosphorylation
body: The electrons of NADH and FADH₂ pass through a chain of carriers in the **inner mitochondrial membrane** down a potential from −0.32 V to +0.82 V, the **electron transport chain**. The sequence is: **Complex I** (NADH dehydrogenase: NADH → FMN → Fe–S clusters → **ubiquinone**, Q; 4 H⁺ pumped); **Complex II** (succinate dehydrogenase, which feeds electrons from FADH₂ to Q; no pumping); **Complex III** (cytochrome bc₁: QH₂ → cytochrome c; 4 H⁺ by the Q-cycle); **Complex IV** (**cytochrome c oxidase**: 4 cytochrome c + O₂ + 4 H⁺ → 2 H₂O; 2–4 H⁺ pumped), where O₂ is reduced completely, with no release of partially reduced, toxic species. Cyanide, azide and CO bind the heme iron of Complex IV and stop respiration.

The energy released drives the pumping of protons from the matrix to the intermembrane space, creating an electrochemical gradient. This is **Mitchell’s chemiosmotic theory**: the gradient, not a chemical intermediate, couples electron transfer to ATP synthesis. The free energy stored is the **proton-motive force**:

body.eq: Δp = Δψ − (2.303RT/F) ΔpH     ΔG (per mol H⁺) = −F·Δp

body: with Δψ ≈ 150–180 mV (matrix negative) and ΔpH ≈ 0.5–1 (matrix alkaline). The **ATP synthase** (F₁F₀) is a rotary motor. Protons flow through the membrane-embedded F₀ part, turning a ring of c subunits (8–15 per ring), which rotates the central γ stalk inside the F₁ head. The rotation (120° steps) drives conformational changes in the three catalytic β subunits (the **binding change mechanism**: loose, tight, open), which bind ADP + Pᵢ, form ATP in the tight state, and release it. With a c-ring of 10 subunits, each ATP needs 10/3 = 3.3 H⁺, and about 1 more H⁺ to import Pᵢ and exchange ATP for ADP across the membrane.

example.title: Energy in the proton gradient
example.problem: Δψ = 160 mV and ΔpH = 0.75 at 37 °C. Find Δp and the energy available per proton. Is ~4 H⁺ per ATP enough to make ATP at ΔG = +55 kJ mol⁻¹?
example.solution: Δp = 160 mV + 61.5 × 0.75 mV = 160 + 46 = 206 mV. Energy per mole of H⁺ = 96.485 × 0.206 = 19.9 kJ. Four protons give 79.5 kJ, more than the 55 kJ needed: efficiency 55/80 = 69%. (Three protons would give 60 kJ, barely enough, so the actual stoichiometry of ~4 H⁺ per ATP gives a margin.)

body: The proton pumping per NADH is ~10 H⁺ (Complexes I, III, IV) and per FADH₂ ~6 H⁺ (III and IV only); dividing by ~4 H⁺ per ATP gives P/O ratios of ≈ 2.5 ATP per NADH and ≈ 1.5 ATP per FADH₂. Cytosolic NADH from glycolysis enters via shuttles (malate–aspartate, ≈ 2.5 ATP, or glycerol phosphate, ≈ 1.5). The bookkeeping for one glucose:

head: Stage
Direct ATP/GTP
NADH
FADH₂
ATP equivalents
table.caption: ATP yield from complete oxidation of glucose (older textbooks give 36–38).

body: The oxidation of glucose has ΔG°′ = −2840 kJ mol⁻¹, and 32 ATP store 32 × 30.5 = 976 kJ: an efficiency of 34% under standard conditions (more at actual concentrations). **Respiratory control** couples the rate of respiration to the demand: with no ADP, the proton gradient builds up and slows the chain. **Uncouplers** (2,4-dinitrophenol, a protonophore that carries H⁺ back across the membrane) dissipate the gradient: respiration speeds up but no ATP is made, and the energy is released as heat. Brown fat uses a natural uncoupling protein (UCP1) for thermogenesis.

check.q: What does the proton-motive force drive?
check.a: ATP synthesis by ATP synthase (and other transport)

check.q: Why does 2,4-dinitrophenol raise the oxygen consumption but lower ATP production?
check.a: It carries protons across the membrane, dissipating the gradient, so respiration runs unchecked without ATP synthesis

check.q: How many ATP are formed per NADH by oxidative phosphorylation (modern estimate)?

sections.title: Photosynthesis
body: **Photosynthesis** uses light to drive the reverse of respiration: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂, ΔG°′ = +2870 kJ mol⁻¹. It takes place in the **chloroplast** (a double-membrane organelle). The **thylakoid** membranes, flattened sacs stacked in grana, hold the light-capturing machinery, and the surrounding **stroma** holds the enzymes of CO₂ fixation. The process has two parts: the **light reactions** (in the thylakoid), which make ATP and NADPH and release O₂; and the **Calvin cycle** (in the stroma), which uses them to reduce CO₂.

Light is absorbed by chlorophylls and carotenoids in **light-harvesting complexes** and the excitation energy is passed (by resonance energy transfer) to a **reaction center**, where the special pair of chlorophyll (P680 in photosystem II, P700 in photosystem I) loses an electron. The two photosystems operate in series, the **Z-scheme**:

list: **Photosystem II**: P680* (E°′ ≈ −0.8 V) donates an electron to pheophytin and on to plastoquinone. The electron lost is replaced by the **oxygen-evolving complex** (a Mn₄CaO₅ cluster), which oxidizes water: 2 H₂O → O₂ + 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻ (four photons per O₂, with the protons released into the thylakoid lumen).
**Cytochrome b₆f** passes electrons from plastoquinol to plastocyanin and pumps protons into the lumen.
**Photosystem I**: P700 absorbs a second photon, and the electron is passed to **ferredoxin** and then by ferredoxin–NADP⁺ reductase to NADP⁺, forming NADPH.

The proton gradient made by water oxidation and by cytochrome b₆f drives the chloroplast ATP synthase (**photophosphorylation**), exactly as in mitochondria but with the orientation reversed. Cyclic electron flow around PSI makes ATP only.

body: The linear electron flow from H₂O to NADP⁺ (ΔE°′ = −0.32 − 0.82 = −1.14 V, uphill by +220 kJ per 2 e⁻) requires two photons per electron, so 8 photons per O₂ (and per CO₂ fixed).

In the Calvin–Benson cycle, **Rubisco** (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase, the most abundant protein on Earth, slow at ~3 s⁻¹ per site) adds CO₂ to the five-carbon **ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP)**, giving two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate (**carbon fixation**). ATP and NADPH then reduce 3-phosphoglycerate to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (G3P), by reactions that are the reverse of glycolysis. Of every 6 G3P formed from 3 CO₂, one leaves as product and 5 are rearranged, using one more ATP each cycle, to regenerate 3 RuBP. Overall, to fix 3 CO₂ into one G3P the cycle uses 9 ATP and 6 NADPH, and for one glucose, 18 ATP and 12 NADPH. The enzymes are regulated by light (through ferredoxin–thioredoxin), so the “dark reactions” run in the light.

Rubisco also reacts with O₂ (**photorespiration**) at a rate that increases with temperature, wasting carbon and energy. C₄ plants (maize, sugarcane) avoid it by first fixing CO₂ into a four-carbon acid in mesophyll cells and releasing it at a high concentration around Rubisco in bundle-sheath cells, at a cost of 2 more ATP per CO₂.

example.title: Efficiency of photosynthesis
example.problem: Making one glucose needs 12 NADPH and 18 ATP, and 48 photons of red light at 680 nm are the theoretical requirement (8 per CO₂). What fraction of the energy of the photons is stored in glucose (ΔG°′ = 2870 kJ mol⁻¹)?
example.solution: Energy of one mole of 680 nm photons = N_A hc/λ = 119,627 kJ nm mol⁻¹/680 nm = 176 kJ. For 48 mol: 48 × 176 = 8450 kJ. Efficiency = 2870/8450 = 34%. In the field, with losses (reflection, saturation, respiration, photorespiration, white light), the efficiency of crops over the season is 1–3%.

check.q: Where does the O₂ released in photosynthesis come from?
check.a: The oxidation of water in photosystem II

check.q: What are the products of the light reactions used by the Calvin cycle?

check.a: It adds CO₂ to ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate (carbon fixation)

quiz.q: A reaction has ΔG°′ = +5.7 kJ mol⁻¹ at 25 °C. What is K′eq?
quiz.why: K′eq = exp(−ΔG°′/RT) = exp(−5700/2478) = exp(−2.30) = 0.10. A positive ΔG°′ means K′eq < 1, so 10 has the wrong sign, and 0.005 results from using log₁₀ instead of ln.

quiz.q: Under standard conditions, which compound cannot donate its phosphate group to ADP to make ATP?
quiz.why: Only compounds whose hydrolysis is more exergonic than that of ATP (−30.5 kJ mol⁻¹) can phosphorylate ADP. Glucose 6-phosphate lies lower on the scale, so ATP phosphorylates glucose rather than the reverse.

quiz.q: E°′ is −0.185 V for pyruvate/lactate and −0.320 V for NAD⁺/NADH. What is ΔG°′ for NADH + pyruvate → NAD⁺ + lactate (n = 2)?
quiz.why: ΔE°′ = −0.185 − (−0.320) = +0.135 V, so ΔG°′ = −nFΔE°′ = −2 × 96.485 × 0.135 = −26 kJ mol⁻¹. Using n = 1 halves it, and subtracting the potentials the wrong way gives −97.

quiz.q: Which three glycolytic enzymes catalyze steps that are irreversible in the cell and must be bypassed in gluconeogenesis?
wrong: Phosphoglucose isomerase, aldolase and pyruvate kinase
quiz.why: These three steps have large negative ΔG and are the control points of the pathway. The other reactions operate near equilibrium and run in either direction.

quiz.q: How much CO₂ and net ATP does the alcoholic fermentation of one glucose by yeast give?
quiz.why: Glycolysis nets 2 ATP, and pyruvate decarboxylase releases one CO₂ from each of the two pyruvates on the way to ethanol. Lactate fermentation would give the same ATP but no CO₂, and 6 CO₂ with 32 ATP is complete respiration.

quiz.a: The oxidation and phosphorylation of glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate
wrong: The phosphorylation of glucose by hexokinase
The transfer of phosphate from PEP to ADP by pyruvate kinase
The cleavage of fructose 1,6-bisphosphate by aldolase
quiz.why: G3P dehydrogenase oxidizes G3P with NAD⁺ and Pᵢ to give 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate and NADH, twice per glucose. The kinase steps transfer phosphate and the aldolase step is a cleavage with no redox change.

quiz.q: Counting the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction and the citric acid cycle together, how many CO₂ are released per glucose oxidized completely?
quiz.why: Two pyruvates give 2 CO₂ in the PDH reaction, and the two acetyl-CoA give 2 CO₂ each in the cycle (isocitrate and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenases), 2 + 4 = 6, all six carbons of glucose.

quiz.q: Citrate is withdrawn from the mitochondrion for fatty acid synthesis. What keeps the cycle from running down?
quiz.a: Anaplerotic reactions such as pyruvate carboxylase, which makes oxaloacetate
wrong: Acetyl-CoA is converted directly back into oxaloacetate
Aconitase makes new citrate from acetyl-CoA alone
Succinate dehydrogenase regenerates the withdrawn carbons
quiz.why: The cycle works only if oxaloacetate and the other intermediates are present as catalysts. Anaplerotic reactions refill them from pyruvate, whereas the two carbons of acetyl-CoA are lost as CO₂ and give no net oxaloacetate.

quiz.q: Which conditions activate the regulated dehydrogenases of the cycle (PDH, isocitrate DH, α-ketoglutarate DH)?
quiz.why: These enzymes are inhibited by NADH and ATP (energy is plentiful) and activated by ADP and Ca²⁺ (muscle work), so the rate follows demand.

quiz.q: Δψ = 140 mV and ΔpH = 0.6 across the inner mitochondrial membrane at 37 °C. What is Δp?
quiz.why: Δp = Δψ − (2.303RT/F)ΔpH, with the ΔpH term written so that it adds to Δψ when the matrix is alkaline: 140 + 61.5 × 0.6 = 177 mV. Subtracting gives 103 mV, and ignoring the pH term gives 140 mV.

quiz.q: Why does an electron pair from FADH₂ support fewer ATP (≈ 1.5) than one from NADH (≈ 2.5)?
quiz.a: FADH₂ enters at Complex II, bypassing Complex I, so about 6 H⁺ are pumped instead of 10
wrong: FADH₂ also feeds Complex I, but only one of its two electrons is used
FADH₂ has a more negative potential than NADH, so less energy is released
Complex II pumps 4 H⁺ and Complex III none, giving a smaller gradient
quiz.why: Succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II) passes electrons to ubiquinone without pumping protons, so only Complexes III and IV pump. At about 4 H⁺ per ATP, 6 H⁺ gives ≈ 1.5 ATP and 10 H⁺ gives ≈ 2.5.

quiz.q: Cyanide binds the heme iron of Complex IV. What is the immediate result?
quiz.a: Electron flow stops, O₂ consumption falls and NADH accumulates
wrong: O₂ consumption rises, but no ATP is made, as with an uncoupler
Protons leak back across the membrane and the gradient collapses
Electron flow continues normally, but ATP synthase is blocked
quiz.why: Complex IV is the only site where electrons reduce O₂, so blocking it halts the entire chain and proton pumping. An uncoupler such as dinitrophenol instead speeds respiration while dissipating the gradient.

quiz.q: A resting cell stops using ATP, so its ADP level falls. What happens to its O₂ consumption?
quiz.a: It falls, because Δp builds up and slows electron transport
wrong: It rises, to make more ATP from the available substrate
It stays constant, because electron transport is independent of ATP synthase
It rises, because the cell is now acting like one with an uncoupler
quiz.why: This is respiratory control: with no ADP, protons cannot flow back through ATP synthase, the gradient rises and the chain slows. An uncoupler removes this restraint by providing another route for protons.

quiz.q: An ATP synthase has a c-ring of 8 subunits. How many H⁺ pass through it per ATP made, ignoring transport costs?
quiz.why: One full rotation of the c-ring moves 8 protons and produces 3 ATP, one at each of the three catalytic β subunits. The ratio is therefore c/3, as with 10/3 = 3.3 for a 10-subunit ring.

quiz.q: What is the minimum number of photons needed in linear electron flow to release 3 O₂ from water?
quiz.why: Water oxidation gives 4 e⁻ per O₂, and each electron passes through both photosystems and so needs two photons: 8 photons per O₂ and 24 for three.

quiz.q: How much ATP and NADPH does the Calvin cycle consume per CO₂ fixed?
quiz.why: Fixing 3 CO₂ into one G3P costs 9 ATP and 6 NADPH, so per CO₂ the cost is 3 ATP and 2 NADPH. The 9 and 6 are the cost per G3P.

quiz.q: Where do the protons come from that drive the chloroplast ATP synthase?
quiz.a: Water oxidation and cytochrome b₆f put them into the thylakoid lumen, and they flow out to the stroma through the synthase
wrong: Photosystem I pumps them from the lumen into the stroma
Rubisco releases them in the stroma while fixing CO₂
They accumulate in the stroma and flow into the lumen through the synthase
quiz.why: Splitting water releases 4 H⁺ per O₂ into the lumen and cytochrome b₆f pumps more; the resulting lumen-to-stroma gradient drives photophosphorylation, like the mitochondrial system with the orientation reversed.

quiz.q: How do C₄ plants reduce photorespiration?
quiz.a: They fix CO₂ first into a four-carbon acid, then release it at high concentration around Rubisco
wrong: They lack Rubisco and use a different carboxylase
They run photosystem I alone, so no O₂ is produced near Rubisco
They keep their stomata open so O₂ escapes from the leaf
quiz.why: Rubisco also reacts with O₂, wasting energy, especially when hot. C₄ plants fix CO₂ in mesophyll cells and release it in bundle-sheath cells, raising the CO₂/O₂ ratio at Rubisco, at a cost of 2 more ATP per CO₂.

summary: ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln Q. Coupling to ATP hydrolysis (−30.5 kJ mol⁻¹ standard, −50 to −65 in cells) drives unfavorable reactions. ΔG°′ = −nFΔE°′ links redox potentials to free energy; NADH → O₂ releases 219 kJ mol⁻¹.
Glycolysis: glucose → 2 pyruvate, net 2 ATP + 2 NADH, regulated at PFK-1; fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ (lactate or ethanol).
Pyruvate dehydrogenase gives acetyl-CoA; each turn of the citric acid cycle yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP, 2 CO₂.
The respiratory chain pumps protons to build Δp = Δψ − 61.5 ΔpH (mV); ATP synthase (rotary, ~3.3 H⁺ per ATP plus transport) gives ≈ 2.5 ATP per NADH, 1.5 per FADH₂, ≈ 32 ATP per glucose.
Photosynthesis: PSII (water oxidation) and PSI in series (Z-scheme) make ATP and NADPH; the Calvin cycle (Rubisco) fixes 3 CO₂ with 9 ATP and 6 NADPH per G3P. Maximum efficiency ≈ 34%.

problems.q: In a muscle cell [ATP] = 5.0 mM, [ADP] = 0.50 mM and [Pᵢ] = 5.0 mM at 310 K. Calculate ΔG for ATP hydrolysis (ΔG°′ = −30.5 kJ mol⁻¹).
The reaction malate + NAD⁺ → oxaloacetate + NADH has ΔG°′ = +29.7 kJ mol⁻¹ (K′ = 6 × 10⁻⁶), yet it proceeds in the citric acid cycle. How?
problems.solution: In the matrix, the next step of the cycle (citrate synthase, ΔG°′ ≈ −32 kJ mol⁻¹) removes oxaloacetate at once, so [oxaloacetate] is kept very low (~10⁻⁷ M), and NADH is reoxidized by the respiratory chain, keeping NADH/NAD⁺ low. With Q very small, ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln Q becomes ≈ 0 or negative. This is the principle of a metabolic pathway: the sum of the steps is strongly favorable and pulls each unfavorable step.
problems.a: Product removal by the next, strongly exergonic step keeps Q small.

problems.q: Calculate the ATP yield from the complete oxidation of one molecule of palmitic acid (C₁₆) to CO₂: β-oxidation produces 7 FADH₂, 7 NADH and 8 acetyl-CoA, and 2 ATP equivalents are used to activate the fatty acid.
problems.solution: 7 FADH₂ × 1.5 = 10.5; 7 NADH × 2.5 = 17.5; 8 acetyl-CoA × 10 (3 NADH × 2.5 + 1 FADH₂ × 1.5 + 1 GTP) = 80. Total = 108 − 2 (activation) = 106 ATP.

problems.q: A chloroplast thylakoid lumen has pH 4.5 and the stroma pH 7.5. Taking Δψ ≈ 0, find the proton-motive force at 25 °C, and the minimal number of protons per ATP if ΔG for ATP synthesis in the chloroplast is +50 kJ mol⁻¹.
problems.solution: ΔpH = 3.0; Δp = 59.2 × 3.0 = 178 mV. Energy per proton = 96.485 × 0.178 = 17.2 kJ mol⁻¹. Protons per ATP ≥ 50/17.2 = 2.9, so at least 3; the chloroplast ATP synthase (c₁₄ ring, 14/3 = 4.7 H⁺ per ATP) works with a large margin.
problems.a: Δp = 178 mV; at least 3 H⁺ per ATP.
